summary.text: A magnetic field is a property of space that tells you how strong the magnetic influence is at each location.
Because strength and direction both change from place to place, it is described by assigning an arrow-like vector to every point in space.
Motors, generators, transformers, electromagnets and inductors are all designed around magnetic fields.

facts.label: Unit of field strength
facts.value: The tesla, with 1 tesla equal to 10,000 gauss

facts.label: Measuring instrument
facts.value: A magnetometer measures the local magnetic field

facts.label: Finest precision reached
facts.value: Gravity Probe B reached 5 aT (5×10⁻¹⁸ T)

facts.label: Field line rule
facts.value: Closer lines mean a stronger field

facts.label: Compass behaviour
facts.value: A small compass points along the field line

items.prompt: On a weather-style map of a magnet's surroundings, why must each point carry an arrow and not only a number?

options.label: Because the field has a direction as well as a strength
Because the strength is always the same everywhere
Because the arrow shows the temperature of the magnet
Because numbers cannot be measured in space

items.explain: Both the strength and the direction of a magnetic field can change with location, so it is a vector field.

items.prompt: In a picture of field lines around a magnet, you see the lines crowded together near one end and spread out far away. What does that tell you?

options.label: The field is weaker where the lines crowd together
The field is the same, only the drawing differs
The field is stronger where the lines are closer
The field is zero where the lines are spread out

items.explain: The strength of the field is proportional to how close the lines are. A different drawing resolution would show more or fewer lines, though.

items.prompt: You place a tiny compass at one point near a magnet. Which description of its needle is right?

options.label: It points along the field line passing through that spot
It points straight at the nearest edge of the magnet
It points across the field line at a right angle
It spins freely because there is no preferred direction

items.explain: A small compass points in the direction of the field line, which is tangent to the field there.

items.prompt: An engineer wants to detect a magnetic field that is rising and falling, not constant. Which kind of magnetometer would work for that job only?

options.label: A Hall effect magnetometer
A SQUID magnetometer
A fluxgate magnetometer
An induction (search-coil) magnetometer

items.explain: Induction or search-coil magnetometers measure only varying fields, while the other kinds listed can measure other cases too.

items.prompt: A power company explains why it needs to understand magnetic fields. Which reason fits what the field is used for?

options.label: Fields are used to make wires colder and thinner
Fields are central to how generators and transformers are designed
Fields decide how much gas each plant burns
Fields are used to store electric charge in batteries

items.explain: Magnetic fields matter in the design and use of electric motors, generators, transformers, electromagnets and inductors.

items.prompt: Astronomers cannot send a probe to a distant star's field. How can they still detect it?

options.label: By watching how it changes the colour of starlight only
By bouncing a compass needle off the star
By weighing the star to find its magnetism
By seeing its effect on nearby charged particles, such as radio emission

items.explain: Distant fields are measured through their effects on local charged particles, for example electrons spiralling around a field line give off detectable synchrotron radiation.
